knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)

Let's study how extreme temperatures may influence coffee production.

## Unit of analysis

What is the unit of analysis in this dataset?

## Visualizing panel data

Let's visualize coffee production against average annual temperatures.

How do you interpret the plot below --- What is happening to `avgTemp` over the years? What about `ln_coffee_prod`? 

```{r scatter-coffee-temp-year}
ggplot(coffee, aes(x = avgTemp, y = ln_coffee_prod, colour = year)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_colour_gradientn(
  colours = c(
    "#E8D3B0",  # Latte
    "#C9A47E",  # Cappuccino
    "#A47148",  # Caramel
    "#70452C",  # Mocha
    "#3B2418"   # Espresso
  ),
  name = "Year",
  breaks = unique(c(
    min(coffee$year, na.rm = TRUE),
    seq(min(coffee$year, na.rm = TRUE),
        max(coffee$year, na.rm = TRUE), by = 15)
    ))
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

```

If you hover over the points in the plot below, you'll see an informational pop-up. 

What can you say about the differences across countries, and within countries over time? Can you tell whether temperatures might be influencing coffee production from this plot?

```{r scatter-coffee-temp-countries}

coffee_cols <- c(
  "#E8D3B0",  # Latte
  "#C9A47E",  # Cappuccino
  "#A47148",  # Caramel
  "#70452C",  # Mocha
  "#3B2418"   # Espresso
)

plot_ly(
  data = coffee,
  x = ~avgTemp,
  y = ~ln_coffee_prod,
  type = "scattergl",
  mode = "markers",
  color = ~year,
  colors = coffee_cols,
  marker = list(
    size = 5,
    opacity = 0.7
  ),
  text = ~paste0(
    "Country: ", countryCode,
    "<br>Year: ", year,
    "<br>Temperature: ", round(avgTemp, 2),
    "<br>Log production: ", round(ln_coffee_prod, 2)
  ),
  hoverinfo = "text"
) %>%
  layout(
    xaxis = list(title = "Average Temperature"),
    yaxis = list(title = "Log Coffee Production"),
    plot_bgcolor = "white",
    paper_bgcolor = "white"
  ) %>%
  config(
    displaylogo = FALSE,
    displayModeBar = FALSE
  )
```


The average temperature per year in a country may hide fluctuations in a given year, say, across months. So we'll use `dummy_min4_xtremeMonths`.
What does the dummy `dummy_min4_xtremeMonths` mean?

Let's visualize this. 

```{r scatter-coffee-dummy-year}
ggplot(coffee, aes(x = dummy_min4_xtremeMonths, y = ln_coffee_prod, colour = year)) +
  geom_point() +

  # Mean points
  stat_summary(
  fun = mean,
  geom = "point",
  colour = "black",
  size = 3
  ) +

  # 95% CI error bars
  stat_summary(
  fun.data = \(y) {
    n <- sum(!is.na(y))
    m <- mean(y, na.rm = TRUE)
    se <- sd(y, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n)
    ci <- qt(0.975, df = n - 1) * se

    data.frame(
      y = m,
      ymin = m - ci,
      ymax = m + ci
    )
  },
  geom = "errorbar",
  colour = "black",
  width = 0.1,
  linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_colour_gradientn(
  colours = c(
    "#E8D3B0",  # Latte
    "#C9A47E",  # Cappuccino
    "#A47148",  # Caramel
    "#70452C",  # Mocha
    "#3B2418"   # Espresso
  ),
  name = "Year",
  breaks = unique(c(
    min(coffee$year, na.rm = TRUE),
    seq(min(coffee$year, na.rm = TRUE),
        max(coffee$year, na.rm = TRUE), by = 15)
    ))
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 1)) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

```

## Interpreting coefficients

Take a moment, and using the regression below, compare the Estimate column for the Intercept and `dummy_min4_xtremeMonths` with the plot above. How do you interpret the coefficient? 

```{r reg-coffee-dummy}
m1 <- feols(ln_coffee_prod ~ dummy_min4_xtremeMonths, data = coffee, vcov = ~countryCode)
summary(m1)
```

Note for Sushil: Derive log interpretation in class. 

How would you interpret this if it was -0.078 instead?

## Adding year fixed effects

What do you learn from the estimation of the model below?

```{r reg-coffee-dummy-yfe}
# run a fixed effects regression with year fixed effects
m2 <- feols(ln_coffee_prod ~ dummy_min4_xtremeMonths | year, data = coffee, vcov = ~countryCode)
summary(m2)
```

## Adding country fixed effects

Take a moment: this code will work, but it's wrong as it doesn't have country fixed effects. Add country fixed effects and estimate this model.

```{r reg-coffee-dummy-yfe-cfe}
# run a fixed effects regression with year and country fixed effects
m3 <- feols(ln_coffee_prod ~ dummy_min4_xtremeMonths | year, data = coffee, vcov = ~countryCode)
summary(m3)
```

What do you learn from the estimation of the model above? It might help to use the "within" framework in your explanation.

## Same regression done differently

What have we done in this regression and why is the estimate for `dummy_min4_xtremeMonths` the same as before? 

```{r reg-coffee-dummy-yfe-mundlak}
coffee <- coffee %>%
  group_by(countryCode) %>%
  mutate(countryavg_dummy = mean(dummy_min4_xtremeMonths, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup()

m4 <- feols(ln_coffee_prod ~ dummy_min4_xtremeMonths + countryavg_dummy | year, data = coffee, vcov = ~countryCode)
summary(m4) 
```


The Mundlak term accounts for cross-country averages. If you recall the interpretation of dummy variables, and the Least Square Dummy Variable (LSDV) interpretation, it ALSO accounts for cross-country averages!

## Choosing the right model.

Based on the Mundlak regression, which model would you choose from the ones we've done?

What is your conclusion about the effect of extreme temperatures on coffee production?

We had imperfect temperature data for this analysis. A month with an average of 24 degree temperature, could be either due to (1) a bad month: 2 weeks of 27 degrees and 2 weeks of 21 degrees; or (2) a good month: all 4 weeks with 24 degrees. That is, some of the dummies stored as 0s may not precisely measure our object of interest which is --- was it a bad month for coffee production temperature-wise?

The analysis still tells us that at an aggregate level, the climate hasn't affected coffee production much amongst countries that were already coffee producers. Again, that is probably not saying much as the coffee producers might be getting hotter, but still have stayed within the 18-26 range from 1961-2024, and it's possible that we still haven't seen the worst of climate change yet.
